1: vicinae is a multi purpose launcher built with QtQuick. This file focuses on explaining general rules. For everything else, just look at the codebase.
2: 
3: It uses QML for presentation and C++ for business logic.
4: React/Typescript is used to power the extension API.
5: 
6: For development: 
7: - On UNIXes, use `make dev`.
8: - On Windows use `cmake --preset windows-relwithdebinfo` (full debug builds only when needed)
9: 
10: ## Separation of concerns
11: 
12: QML is exclusively used for presentation. DO NOT put business logic inside QML files.
13: It's okay to make small JavaScript functions and utilities as long as their purpose is to help deal with presentation concerns.
14: 
15: To implement views, we use a bridge pattern: a C++ "view host" class exposes data and actions as `Q_PROPERTY`s and `Q_INVOKABLE`s, and a QML component binds to them.
16: 
17: Remain pragmatic about this, we don't want to go back and forth between QML and C++ to execute 2 lines of logic. But most of the time, the separation is clear.
18: 
19: ## C++/QT coding rules
20: 
21: We use C++23 so we have access to most modern C++ features. 
22: Here are a few rules to keep in mind:
23: 
24: - Lack of value: use `std::optional` instead of arbitrary value discriminants such as the empty string. If this is not possible or goes against a commonly used convention, respect the convention first, no shoehorning. If we are dealing with raw pointers, the nullable component is already part of it so no need to add a layer of indirection.
25: - Prefer `std::array` to C arrays where it makes sense. You can use `std::to_array` to initialize them automatically sized from an initializer list.
26: - C symbols: always use the `std::` prefix for symbols coming from C headers (`std::uint64_t`, `std::size_t`, `std::memset`, `std::getenv`, ...) and include the `<c*>` header form. POSIX-only symbols (`ssize_t`, `recv`, ...) have no `std::` counterpart and stay unprefixed.
27: - use `constexpr` and `consteval` as much as possible, we want to move what we can at compile time.
28: - Avoid raw pointers: unless we are dealing with QT's ownership model or a C API. For QT classes that are not QObjects, you should probably use standard smart pointers as recommended in modern QT. 
29: - QObjects must be deleted using `deleteLater` and never raw `delete`, as this can cause memory corruption with signal and slots. Calling `delete` on a `QObject` is a **STRONG** code smell.
30: - Watch for implicit copies: avoid copies as much as possible, use non owning containers when you can (`std::span`, `std::string_view`, `QStringView`) and just `std::move` the data when applicable. When copy is the safest option, use copy: don't go out of your way to respect this rule.
31: - QT vs STL classes: prefer STL containers over QT counterparts.
32: - vectors: always reserve `std::vector`s and use `emplace_back` to push new elements.
33: - STL ranges: we like to use `<ranges>` where it works well. If you need to use a `for` loop, prioritize ranged ones or use `std::views::enumerate` if you need to deal with indexes and data.
34: - casts: as you may notice from the clang-tidy rules, using `static_cast` is generally discouraged for classes that are related by inheritance, as it is very easy to make mistakes. Unless the logic is in a hot path (e.g a QT event filter), it's preferrable to use `dynamic_cast` as a safety net when there is no safer option. Note however that `dynamic_cast` is STILL a code smell and should generally be avoided in favor of better polymorphism.
35: - Platform guards: use Qt's `Q_OS_*` macros (`Q_OS_MACOS`, `Q_OS_LINUX`, `Q_OS_WIN`) rather than `Q_OS_DARWIN` or compiler-defined ones like `__APPLE__`. `Q_OS_MACOS` specifically targets desktop macOS (excluding iOS/tvOS) and keeps guards consistent across the codebase.
36: - As Vicinae becomes cross-platform, it is really important that we implement functionality the way it is intended to on the target platform. We should avoid using weird hacks and always use native APIs when possible.
37: 
38: ## Coding style
39: 
40: - For QObject classes: always put `Q_OBJECT`, `Q_PROPERTY`, `Q_INVOKABLE`, and `signals` on top of the class, in this order.
41: - Do not add unnecessary comments. Use them sparingly when something really needs to be made explicit.
42: - Include order: system headers before local headers.
43: - Header guards: use `#pragma once`.
44: - String types: use `std::string` internally, `QString` only at the Qt boundary.
45: - Constants: use `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` for `constexpr` and `static const` values.
46: - Do not overuse comments, only add them when they provide actual value
47: 
48: ## Linting and formatting
49: 
50: We format all our code using `clang-format`. We have a `make format` rule that will automatically format the entire codebase if necessary.
51: 
52: To format the codebase:
53: 
54: - On UNIXes, run `make format`
55: - On Windows, run the PowerShell script at `.\scripts\format.ps1`
56: 
57: ALWAYS run `make format` at the end of a development session to make sure formatting is properly applied to all files.
58: 
59: All our code is also linted with `clang-tidy` in order to make detecting common mistakes easier. `clang-tidy` violations may be acceptable under some circumstances, and should be implemented using `//NOLINTBEGIN(<rule>)` and `NOLINTEND(<rule>)`. comments. Inline `//NOLINT` comments are generally discouraged because they can break after formatting. If a nolint directive does not work (e.g we're dealing with an internal STL false positive) then you can do a local override of the `clang-tidy` configuration to explicitly disable the faulty check.
60: 
61: ## QML rules
62: 
63: QML code should pass the linter, which you can run using `make qmllint`.
64: 
65: When writing JavaScript inside QML files, use ES6 syntax to the largest extent possible.
66: 
67: Try to keep the amount of logic in these files small. Logic in QML is only for presentation concerns: metrics computation, hover on signal, etc...
68: 
69: Some configuration and theming options may need to be accessed directly in QML. We expose a global config and theme bridges for this use case.
70: 
71: ## Code generation
72: 
73: There are two main families of code generation in the codebase:
74: 
75: - IPC, used by the CLI, the input server, and the extension runtime. This uses our own generator `figura` which is directly compiled in tree and invoked when needed.
76: - Generating of static datasets, such as emoji/symbol lists. We generally generate these using some typescript or python scripts, but do not make them part of the build system. We regenerate the lists from time to time, depending on the usecase. For example we have a `make genicon` and `make emoji` rules.
77: 
78: ## Internationalization
79: 
80: User-visible natural-language strings must be marked for translation. English source text is the translation key.
81: 
82: - QML: wrap literals in `qsTr("...")`.
83: - C++ classes with `Q_OBJECT`: use `tr("...")`.
84: - C++ classes without `Q_OBJECT`: NEVER call the inherited `tr()` (it resolves to the wrong context at runtime). Add `Q_DECLARE_TR_FUNCTIONS(ClassName)` at the top of the class, or for a single string use `QCoreApplication::translate("ClassName", "...")`.
85: - Never store translated strings in `static`/`constexpr` data. Plurals use `tr("%n item(s)", nullptr, n)`. Never concatenate translated fragments: use `%1` placeholders with `.arg()`.
86: - Preserve brand and product names such as "Raycast Store", "Raycast Compat", and "Extension Store". Translate the surrounding prose, not the name itself.
87: - Never translate stable technical notation such as ids, acronyms, unit symbols (`MB`, `GB`), filenames, protocol names, icon names (`ImageURL::builtin`), log output, storage keys, or strings compared as discriminants.
88: - Use natural, concise language appropriate for a desktop launcher. Prefer familiar UI wording over literal translations, bureaucratic language, or an excessively formal or polite tone.
89: - Use the platform's official localized terminology for operating-system features and settings pages.
90: - Use stable explicit translation contexts for shared domain strings. Add translator notes or disambiguation only when the source text is genuinely ambiguous.
91: - Source text and location metadata in `src/server/translations/*.ts` are generated: never hand-edit them. Edit
92:   translations with Qt Linguist. Contributors are not required to translate new strings or include regenerated catalogs in
93:   feature PRs. Maintainers periodically run `make update-translations` in dedicated localization updates.
94: 
95: ## General guidelines
96: 
97: - Search should always be fuzzy, unless it has a good reason not to. We have fuzzy utilities already, and we like to use our fuzzy trait system by specializing the `FuzzySearchable` template
98: - We are building Vicinae with cross-platform compatibility in mind (Linux, MacOS, Windows) so abstractions need to be designed accordingly. While Linux is our main development target, we should avoid making abstractions that are too platform specific.
99: 
100: ## React/TypeScript extensions
101: 
102: Everything related to the Typescript SDK can be found under `src/typescript`. More information can be obtained by reading `README.md` files under this directory if you need to work on this part.

1: This document contains a set of guidelines you need to follow before contributing to vicinae, be it through a bug report or code.
2: 
3: ## Raising issues
4: 
5: All issues are tracked using the built-in GitHub issue tracker. If you are not sure your problem justifies creating a new issue, you can create a GitHub discussion or join the Discord server.
6: 
7: Before opening an issue, do a quick search to make sure you are not creating a duplicate.
8: 
9: Make sure to follow the issue template that is provided. In particular, bug issues should be submitted using the "Report Bug" command from vicinae directly, unless the bug results in the vicinae server not being able to start.
10: 
11: If you want to report a bug relative to an extension published in the official vicinae store, you should open the issue in the [extension repository](https://github.com/vicinaehq/extensions), not in the main vicinae repository.
12: 
13: If you think you've found a severe security issue, you should contact the email address listed as the contact address for the [vicinaehq organization](https://github.com/vicinaehq).
14: 
15: ## Contributing code
16: 
17: ### General guidelines
18: 
19: Less is more: each new line of code represents additional maintenance for the project and huge PRs have lower odds of being accepted, especially if they involve significant architectural commitments that were not discussed before.
20: 
21: If you want to work on a big change, you should probably join the [discord server](https://vicinae.com/discord) and discuss it in the dev channel beforehand.
22: 
23: All submitted code needs to be locally tested. See [this page of the documentation](https://docs.vicinae.com/build) for build instructions and development tips.
24: 
25: ### Formatting and linting
26: 
27: Formatting is done with `clang-format`, as prescribed by the `.clang-format` file present at the root of the repository. Contributions must respect the format. You can run `make format` to apply formatting to all project files at once, but your IDE should be able to pick up on it and automatically format the code.
28: 
29: Keep the number of comments to a strict minimum, good code shouldn't need many comments. There are good use cases for comments though: if you feel like your solution to a given problem is not ideal, could be improved, or relies on a weird hack, using a comment to document it is encouraged. We don't use documentation generators at the moment, so such type of comments are not needed.
30: 
31: A `.clang-tidy` configuration file was added very recently to the project, but it's not currently enforced because a lot of code has yet to be migrated. New code **must** be checked against these rules. Most IDEs should be able to automatically provide intellisense based on the presence of the `.clang-tidy` file alone.
32: 
33: ### AI generated code
34: 
35: AI generated code is treated the same as regular code. As such, all the aforementioned rules apply.
36: 
37: AI is **not** a substitute for properly understanding and testing your code: don't be lazy. Lazy AI PRs that do not respect the guidelines will be rejected. In particular, keep your pull request's description as concise as possible: no maintainer will read your novel.
38: 
39: If your contribution was mostly AI generated, it's considered good practice to indicate what model or tool you used for that.

1: # libglyph
2: 
3: A static table of emoji and curated Unicode symbols, plus emoji-specific helpers.
4: 
5: - `glyph/glyph.hpp` — the table and lookups (`glyph::`).
6: - `glyph/emoji.hpp` — emoji-only helpers: skin tones, segmentation, detection (`emoji::`).
7: 
8: ## Generated data
9: 
10: `src/glyph.cpp`, `include/glyph/glyph.hpp` and `src/emoji-properties.cpp` are
11: generated by `scripts/` from the Unicode Character Database, emoji-test/emoji-data
12: and the CLDR English annotations, then committed. This is not part of the build:
13: regenerate from time to time (new Unicode/Emoji release, curation tweaks) with
14: 
15: ```sh
16: make gen-db   # or `make emoji` from the repo root; needs node >= 22.18 (runs TypeScript directly) and network access
17: ```
18: 
19: `scripts/fetch.ts` downloads the upstream files into `scripts/assets/` (gitignored) and
20: records their versions, which `scripts/gen.ts` stamps into the generated files'
21: first line. Pin a release with `UNICODE_VERSION=17.0.0` / `CLDR_REF=48.2.0`.
22: 
23: What gets included is decided by `scripts/src/curate.ts` (symbol block allowlist
24: and per-category routing) and `scripts/src/categories.ts` (the category list, which
25: is also the source of the `glyph::Category` enum order). Emoji keep the
26: canonical emoji-test order; skin-tone variants are collapsed onto their
27: `skinnable` base and composed at runtime.
28: 
29: `emoji-properties.cpp` holds the emoji binary-property ranges (Emoji,
30: Emoji_Presentation, Emoji_Modifier, Emoji_Modifier_Base) feeding
31: `lookupProperties` in `src/emoji-properties.hpp`, keeping the lib free of any
32: Unicode-property runtime dependency.
33: 
34: ## Emoji segmentation
